diagram_math_checks.result: Every row has vertices A,B,C and exactly edges AB,BC, with no AC edge. This matches the skeleton and unshielded-triple definitions at lines 31–35. Native standalone view confirms three vertices and two edges per row; total 12 displayed vertices and eight edges.

Rows 1–3 are A→B→C, A←B←C, and A←B→C. A path skeleton has no cycle, so all three orientations are DAGs. No row has both arrows into B; thus no new unshielded collider is introduced, as required by lines 43–45.

Two edges each have two orientation choices, giving four orientations. The omitted A→B←C is the only collider orientation. The other three are exactly the consistent extensions of the undirected path. AB is directed A→B in extension 1 and B→A in extensions 2 and 3; BC is B→C in extensions 1 and 3 and C→B in extension 2. Neither edge is compelled, so lines 46–52 give exactly the displayed undirected completed pattern.

Read items/def-d-separation-in-a-dag.md in full. In the three shown DAGs, B is the unique internal vertex of the A–C path and is a noncollider. Hence that path is active for empty conditioning and blocked by {B}. Adjacent endpoint pairs always have a one-edge active path. On this three-vertex set these facts determine all pairwise-disjoint-set d-separations (nonempty separated endpoint sets can only be {A},{C}); empty endpoint cases are vacuous. The collider alternative reverses the empty versus {B} behavior and is therefore outside this class.

The source supplies the graph-orientation and d-separation reasoning in prose outside the diagram. This definition has no Proof section, and its defining clauses are byte-identical. No rigorous argument relies on viewing the figure.
